messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Data Scientist
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Entrapment: Having no options, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Vignette:
Minh Nguyen was eighty years old, a retired data scientist who still consulted part-time from the home he had shared with his late wife, and a man who had spent three years as a relief worker in the highlands of Vietnam during the war. What he saw there had never left him. The moment that played over most often—like a film he could not stop—was the afternoon in a village near Quảng Ngãi when a group of soldiers rounded up the families who had taken shelter in the church. Minh had been helping distribute rice. He watched a young father step forward to plead for his children, and he watched the butt of a rifle swing into the man’s face. There was no way to stop it. The officer in charge had already told the relief team to stay back or be shot. Minh stood frozen, clutching a sack of grain, his options reduced to zero: intervene and die, or watch and carry the image forever. He had done nothing. The memory did not feel like something that happened fifty years ago. It felt like it was happening right now—the heat, the dust, the metallic taste of helplessness, the man’s body crumpling. And the worst part was the replay. The film ran every time he closed his eyes, every time he caught a news report about a conflict somewhere else, every time he saw someone behave cruelly in an ordinary American setting. People misbehaving—a driver shouting at a cyclist, a colleague cutting off a subordinate in a meeting—that was enough to slam him back into the church courtyard, heart hammering, certain that danger was imminent.

Over the decades, Minh had built a careful life to manage the chaos inside him. He had long ago stopped watching the evening news. If a headline about a war or a refugee crisis appeared on his phone, he swiped it away before the first sentence could register. He could not afford to let the images in. But avoidance had grown into something more pervasive. Before every interaction—even a phone call with his daughter in Seattle—Minh rehearsed his lines, word for word, tone for tone. He was terrified that if he spoke spontaneously, his anger would slip out and he would say something terrible, something that would prove he had become the kind of man he feared: violent, out of control. The fear of his own rage had become as loud as the memories themselves. He had come to believe that his reactions since the war meant he was going crazy, that his mind was permanently broken. The world felt saturated with threat. In the grocery store he scanned every aisle for exits, noted the position of each shopper, measured the distance to the door. His body was always tense, always ready—shoulders tight, jaw clenched, hands ready to form fists. Irritability had become his baseline. A long red light, a slow cashier, a misplaced file on his computer—these could trigger a burst of anger that surprised him as much as it alarmed others. He had snapped at his daughter once, two years ago, and had not spoken to her in person since; he rehearsed their conversations now instead of having them.

The nightmares were the worst. He would wake disoriented, the residue of the dream clinging to his skin—the smell of smoke, the sound of crying, the press of bodies—and for a long moment he could not tell whether he was in his bedroom or back in the highlands. That feeling of being trapped, having no options, was more terrifying than the dream itself. And then the negative emotions would flood in: fear, horror, anger, guilt, shame, all at once, and he would lie still, afraid that moving would set off something unstoppable.

He finally called a clinic after a Tuesday morning when a neighbor’s television, too loud through the wall, was broadcasting a documentary about a distant famine. Minh heard the word “refugee” and the film started—the church, the father, the rifle—and he could not stop it. He paced the living room, scanning the windows, rehearsing what he would say if the neighbor knocked, convinced that if he did not control his anger he would do something terrible. When the film finally faded, he sat on the edge of his bed, exhausted, and admitted to himself that the strategies were not working. He was not safe; he was just alone with the memories. Now, in the therapist’s office, he sits with his hands folded, scanning the room for exits, already rehearsing his first sentence. He hopes for a way to quiet the replay, but what he fears most is that talking about the memory will make it real all over again—and that this time, he will not be able to get back up.
